summary: Between-subjects user study: 54 CS students (59 recruited, 5 dropped for attention checks) build a small HTML/CSS/JS game. Group A uses an Aider agent (GPT-4.1) that edits their code; group B uses a GPT-4.1 chatbot restricted to generic snippets. Agent users finish the initial task more accurately and quickly but score much lower on comprehension questions about their own code. Their advantage on a no-agent extension task disappears once initial accuracy is controlled for. Low-effort interaction (copying criteria as prompts, auto-accepting edits) correlates with lower comprehension.

claims.claim: Agents improve initial task completion but harm users' comprehension of their own code.
claims.evidence: Fig. 1/Fig. 4: agent users higher initial accuracy and faster; comprehension much lower (Fig. 1 caption: p<0.002, Cohen's d>0.80). Groups similar on background quiz (Fig. 4a). §4.3 regression: agent group still significantly lower after controlling for initial accuracy.

claims.claim: Agents do not prepare users to extend their code without agents.
claims.evidence: §4.3, Fig. 7: extension accuracy is similar across groups. Initial accuracy and comprehension both predict extension (adj. R² 0.05 -> 0.34); mediation analysis in Appendix A.5. Fig. 1 caption: agent users extend better unadjusted, but this reverses when controlling for initial accuracy.

claims.claim: Low-effort prompting (copy+paste criteria) and auto-accepted edits are linked with lower comprehension.
claims.evidence: Prompt-strategy table in §5.1 (e.g. copying criteria 0.654 comprehension, 25 users; turning criteria into syntax 0.743) and Table 2 (auto-accept vs per-file review). Correlational, with subgroups as small as 5-6 users and background ability differing across strategies.

claims.claim: Users prefer agents despite recognizing weaker understanding.
claims.evidence: §6.1, Table 3 self-reports: agent 'helpful' 4.7 ± 0.2 vs chatbot 3.3 ± 0.2; most prefer the option to switch.

patterns.note: Diff-review approval and execution summaries did not preserve understanding; users who auto-accepted had the lowest comprehension. Approval gates become rubber stamps when reviewers don't understand the code.
Pasting acceptance criteria verbatim as prompts completed the task but correlated with low comprehension. Users who translated criteria into concrete technical instructions understood more.
Relevant tension: spec-to-agent hand-off without engagement may yield working code the owners don't understand.

[retag 2026-10-08] Fig. 1, §4.1: users of an Aider agent that explains its edits and offers per-file review score much lower on comprehension of their own code (p<0.002, d>0.80) than users of a restricted snippet-only chatbot, which acts as a de facto learning mode. The chatbot arm loses on initial accuracy, and extension accuracy is similar once initial accuracy is controlled (§4.3). The agent's own explanations did not protect understanding. Users who asked it to 'explain the whole project' scored 0.635 (n=6, Table 1), and per-file reviewers (0.777, n=7, Table 2) still trailed chatbot users. Comprehension is closed-book recall, and behaviour-impact questions show no gap (App. A.9.2). 54 students, one toy web task.

methodology.sample: 54 analyzed CS students (17 B.S., 31 M.S., 11 Ph.D. among 59 recruited) from two U.S. colleges; one 50-minute web task plus an extension task.
methodology.baselines: Restricted chatbot (no code access, generic snippets) as comparator; no no-AI or unrestricted-chatbot arm.
methodology.models: GPT-4.1 for both arms (Aider agent). GPT-5.2 generates comprehension questions; Gemini-3.1 Pro scores rubrics.
methodology.variance: Regression with 95% CIs, p-values, effect sizes; single task.
methodology.ablations: Regression controls (background ability, initial accuracy); mediation model.
methodology.contamination_controls: Rubric hidden from users; distractor guessability check (0.38 vs 0.5 random); attention checks.

biases.detail: CS students recruited for extra credit, not professional developers working in their own codebases.
One small three-file tic-tac-toe variant built from scratch in 50 minutes; no existing large codebase.
Both arms use GPT-4.1, and the agent is Aider only.
54 participants split in two; the strategy-level analyses rest on 5-25 users per cell.
The chatbot arm is artificially restricted (no code access, syntax-only), so the contrast is agent vs writing-it-yourself, not agent vs a typical chat assistant.

coi.affiliations: University of Maryland, New York University, Carnegie Mellon University.
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Open-source Aider with OpenAI GPT-4.1; no author-owned product. The 'Cursor' vendor hit is only a cited example.
coi.detail: Academic HCI/NLP study; the results are unfavorable to agents, if anything.

verdict_reason: A well-controlled randomized study with validated LLM-assisted measurement and released data, so the comprehension result is credible. However, it uses students, one toy web task, one model, and a restricted comparator. The interaction-strategy findings are correlational.
applicability: Relevant to the team's human-oversight design, though not to the harness mechanics. When engineers hand acceptance criteria to agents and click-approve diffs, they may ship ingestion and delivery code they cannot maintain or debug. That risk is higher across several repositories and in a regulated domain context where reviewers must answer for the content pipeline. Practical takeaways: require reviewers to engage, for example by explaining the change or answering a generated comprehension check in PR review; discourage pasting specs verbatim and ask engineers to refine specs into technical intent; and treat approval gates as insufficient on their own. Transfer is limited: students building toy JavaScript from scratch are not Java backend developers working in existing codebases.

conflicts_with.detail: That position paper argues every goal of code review can be served by agents and that humans reviewing agent code provides no meaningful assurance. This study agrees that diff review by agent users is shallow, especially with auto-accept. But it shows a goal agents cannot serve, human comprehension, is lost and then impairs later unassisted extension, which contradicts the 'every goal' claim.
